title: ‘Artificial Intelligence Is Not Gender-Neutral,’ Third Committee Hears, as Experts Warn of Digital Violence, Backlash against Women’s Rights - UN Meetings Coverage and Press Releases
source: UN Meetings Coverage and Press Releases
content: ‘Artificial Intelligence Is Not Gender-Neutral,’ Third Committee Hears, as Experts Warn of Digital Violence, Backlash against Women’s Rights Artificial intelligence is reproducing and amplifying discrimination against women and girls, the Third Committee (Social, Humanitarian and Cultural) heard today, as experts warned that rapidly evolving technologies are opening new avenues for violence, exploitation and exclusion. “Artificial intelligence (AI) is not gender-neutral. It is built on our data, our histories and our inequalities,” declared Claudia Flores, Chair of the Working Group on discrimination against women and girls. Presenting her report, she warned that AI is transforming how people work, learn, access healthcare and justice, and exercise their rights — but is being developed in societies already marked by profound inequalities. “As a result, AI reflects, reproduces and amplifies discrimination against women and girls,” she said, adding: “Technology must serve human rights and not the other way around.” The digital divide is already shutting women out of opportunities, she continued, with those living in poverty, in rural and Indigenous communities and in conflict-affected areas facing the greatest barriers. “When access to technology is unequal, access to opportunity becomes unequal,” she stressed. Meanwhile, women politicians, journalists and human rights defenders face digital violence and intimidation that undermine democratic participation. Calling for firm limits on AI applications that facilitate gender-based violence, mass surveillance and threats to bodily autonomy, she warned: “Some risks of AI are so grave that no benefit can outweigh them.” “Every one of these harms is much easier to prevent than to repair,” she continued, urging Governments to build human rights safeguards into AI systems from the outset, rather than leaving their development to market forces. “Human rights must be built into AI from its inception,” she declared, calling for women and girls to participate in decisions shaping the digital future. That warning was reinforced by Catarina Carvalho, Director of Intergovernmental Support at the United Nations Entity for Gender Equality and the Empowerment of Women (UN-Women), who reported that, at the current pace, it will take 171 years to achieve Sustainable Development Goal 5 on gender equality. Digital technologies are creating new pathways for trafficking and exploitation while outpacing existing protections, she said, adding: “Criminal justice responses have not kept pace with change.” The slow pace of progress towards eliminating female genital mutilation is similarly alarming, she said, noting that it must accelerate 27-fold to meet the 2030 target; otherwise an estimated 22.7 million additional girls will undergo the practice by then. Resistance to abandoning it is becoming more organized and politicized, she emphasized, calling for stronger legislation, accountability and prevention. Nahla Haidar, Chair of the Committee on the Elimination of Discrimination against Women, warned that persistent economic and social inequalities generated by wars and armed conflicts, humanitarian crises, disasters and the accelerating impacts of climate change are not gender neutral. “Women and girls face heightened risks of displacement, poverty, sexual and gender-based violence, loss of livelihoods, exclusion from decision-making, and disruption of access to health, education and essential services,” she said. For Reem Alsalem, Special Rapporteur on violence against women and girls, its causes and consequences, another neglected dimension of discrimination lies in the lives of older women who are largely invisible in laws, policies, data-collection and public discourse. “Many women carry into later life the accumulated consequences of discrimination and violence experienced throughout their lives,” she said, pointing to the heightened vulnerability of widows, women accused of witchcraft and those living with disability or experiencing statelessness or incarceration. Economic disadvantage compounds that exposure: “A lifetime of lower wages, unpaid care work, interrupted employment and unequal access to property can become poverty and dependency in old age, leaving some women unable to escape abuse or exercise real autonomy.” The human cost of inadequate healthcare was brought into sharp focus by Catharina Boehme, Deputy Executive Director for Programme of the United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA). For every maternal death, 20 to 30 women suffer life-altering childbirth-related injuries, infections or disabilities, she reported. An estimated 500,000 women and girls across 55 low- and middle-income countries live with obstetric fistula, around 90 per cent of them in sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia. “The costs of fistula extend far beyond physical suffering… they ripple through families, communities and national economies,” she said. Over 153,000 women and girls have received fistula repair surgery with UNFPA support, she reported, pointing to a global roadmap intended to accelerate country-led action towards ending the condition by 2030. ‘The Shame Must Shift Sides’ In the ensuing interactive dialogue, delegates underscored the breadth of the challenges facing women and girls, both online and offline, calling for stronger digital safeguards and accountability for perpetrators. “The shame must shift sides,” Luxembourg’s youth delegate declared, relaying the message of young people affected by deepfakes. “It should be felt by those who create and disseminate the content and not the victims. The responsibility lies with platforms that allow it to circulate,” she stated. Even where legislation criminalizes such abuse, its impact is not necessarily felt on the ground, she warned. Algorithms exposing boys to misogynistic online communities pose another threat: “Tomorrow’s violence is being shaped in today’s social media fields.” Norway’s representative cited research indicating that 7 in 10 women have experienced online violence, while 98 per cent of deepfakes are pornographic and 99 per cent of those target women. Malaysia’s delegate asked how Governments could keep legislation responsive to emerging AI-enabled harms. Uruguay’s representative warned that technology has “changed the face of trafficking”, making exploitation harder to detect. “The cross-border nature of the problem shows that no State can deal with this alone,” she stressed, calling for stronger international standards. Nigeria’s delegate similarly urged greater cooperation to prevent technology from facilitating trafficking, violence and discrimination, while harnessing its potential to empower women and girls. Violence Hidden Behind Closed Doors Other speakers drew attention to violence and exclusion that often escape public scrutiny. Cameroon’s representative asked how national reporting systems could uncover, investigate and prosecute abuse against older women isolated in private homes or institutional care. Papua New Guinea’s delegate spotlighted violence linked to accusations of sorcery, to which older women are particularly vulnerable. The Government’s 2024–2029 action plan focuses on prevention, victim protection and access to justice, she said, highlighting cooperation with civil society and faith-based organizations. Angola’s representative said an estimated 20,000 women in her country may be living with obstetric fistula, particularly in rural areas. Ending the condition is a national priority, she stressed, calling for predictable financing and technical assistance. Congo’s delegate likewise highlighted persistent barriers to social services for women and girls in rural communities. The scale of violence remains staggering, the observer for the Sovereign Order of Malta said, citing United Nations estimates that 840 million women have experienced physical or sexual violence in their lifetimes, while 137 women and girls are killed each day in acts of femicide. Also today, in its general debate, the Committee addressed the promotion and protection of human rights; the elimination of racism, racial discrimination, xenophobia and related intolerance, and the right of peoples to self-determination; and issues concerning refugees, returnees and displaced persons, including the report of the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees and humanitarian questions.

title: World Development Report 2026: The Promise of Artificial Intelligence - INSIGHTS IAS
content: Context: Union Minister for Electronics and IT launched the World Bank Group’s flagship World Development Report 2026: The Promise of Artificial Intelligence in New Delhi, jointly hosted by MeitY’s IndiaAI Mission. About The World Development Report (WDR) 2026: What it is? - The annual flagship research publication of the World Bank Group, serving as an authoritative global guide on key development policy issues. The 2026 edition, titled The Promise of Artificial Intelligence, analyzes the macro-developmental opportunities, labor disruptions, and structural prerequisites of AI for low- and middle-income countries. Organisations Associated: - Published by: The World Bank Group. - India Launch Partner: IndiaAI Mission under the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY), Government of India. Key Findings of the Report: - Adopt and Adapt Strategy: Advises developing countries to adopt existing open-access AI models and customise them for local languages and developmental needs, rather than investing heavily in expensive frontier models. - Automation Risk and Job Displacement: Finds that just over 4% of Indian jobs face immediate automation risks, compared with over one-third in advanced economies, while entry-level BPO job postings in South Asia have declined by approximately 20%. - Risks of Excessive Fiscal Subsidies: Warns that generous incentives, including India’s 20-year tax holiday for foreign data centres, could strain public finances, increase electricity costs and disproportionately benefit multinational corporations. - Limits of AI Sovereignty: Emphasises that domestic data centres alone cannot guarantee technological independence, as countries remain dependent on imported advanced semiconductors, specialised cloud infrastructure and global supply chains. - Brain Drain of AI Talent: Highlights India’s net loss of 200 elite AI researchers and inventors during 2011–2024, despite possessing the world’s second-largest AI talent pool of approximately 50,460 professionals in 2025. - Global South’s AI Preparedness Gap: Reveals that only one of 25 low-income economies has an active national AI strategy, highlighting significant disparities in institutional readiness and AI governance capabilities. - Public Perception and AI Regulation: Finds that only 18.8% of Indians express concern about AI, compared with 50.5% in the US, reflecting greater optimism and preference for flexible regulatory guidelines. Significance: - Encourages governments to move beyond isolated pilot projects towards population-scale AI applications, leveraging digital public infrastructure such as AgriStack and AI-based weather forecasting. - Highlights how multilingual, voice-enabled AI tools can address shortages of skilled professionals in healthcare, agriculture and education, particularly among digitally underserved communities.

title: Author or artificial intelligence? Literature in crisis - DW.com
content: It's the hot-button topic at the Frankfurt Book Fair: How profoundly will artificial intelligence (AI) transform the book industry, and how can this transformation be regulated? Given the warnings about the technology's long-term risks to humanity as a whole, such debates might appear rather narrow in scope. In reality, however, they concern very concrete issues — copyright protection, the power of tech giants and the future of creativity. Many agree that the political measures taken don't go far enough. This year, however, another aspect has entered the debate: Can we actually recognize when a text has been written with the help of artificial intelligence, and if so, can this be proven? These are some of the questions raised by the current scandal surrounding Haitian-Canadian author Thelyson Orelien and his debut novel, "C'etait ca ou mourir," (This title means "It Was Either That or Die" in English but an English translation has not yet been published), which was published in Canada in the spring. The book about global migration was universally acclaimed, with translation rights sold in more than 20 languages. Soon after the book was published in France, it was longlisted for the prestigious Prix Goncourt. But then, all of a sudden, allegations emerged that the book had been written almost entirely using AI. Orelien, a rising literary star, found himself branded a fraud despite denying all the allegations. His nomination for the Goncourt was withdrawn. So, who should we believe? An author or an AI that claims to have identified AI-generated writing? When the origins of texts become uncertain "We will have to learn to live with doubt," says Hannes Bajohr, a professor of German literature at the University of California, Berkeley. He has spent years examining how AI is changing both writing and reading. His prediction: If the origins of texts can no longer be reliably established, we will have to evaluate them differently. What matters will be their quality alone, rather than whether AI was used in the writing process. Nina George, a best-selling author and the honorary president of the European Writers' Council, is unwilling to accept this. At the Frankfurt Book Fair, she was awarded the Friedrich Perthes Prize in recognition of her commitment to issues such as AI and copyright reform. George has addressed the European Parliament and the German Bundestag, speaking and writing tirelessly about the dangers of AI models. It is perverse, she says, that an author should suddenly have to prove that their writing is the creation of a human. The focus of her campaigns are the tech corporations' self-serving mentality and copyright protection. Can anyone become an author with AI? But what if an author sees AI not as an enemy but as a tool that makes writing easier? US author and artist Luke Stoffel deliberately used AI in his memoir, "How To Win One Million Dollars and Shit Glitter," and was open about doing so. "I'm dyslexic," he said in a video interview. "I've always written and made up stories, but I never dared to take them any further." It was only with the help of AI, he said, that he was able to fulfill his dream. The technology drew his attention to weaknesses in his writing and suggested a marketing strategy that actually worked. In May 2026, he received an award from the Independent Book Publishers Association (IBPA) for the book. For South African author Coral Hart, AI is actually the foundation of her business model. Publishing under various pseudonyms, each year she releases more than 200 different novels, spanning the genres of romance, thriller and mystery. She sees herself as an ideas person, as well as an editor and publisher. Although none of her books has yet become a bestseller, the business is profitable, she says, and each book reaches more than 5,000 people according to her. Many publishers already working with AI Stoffel considers the entire debate hypocritical and points out that many publishers have been working with AI tools for some time. He's certain that "right now, a million-copy bestseller is being printed that was created with the help of AI. The author won't admit it, and then there'll be a scandal." It is entirely possible that the scandal surrounding Thelyson Orelien is precisely that story. But we may never know for sure. For now, the battle against the tech giants continues, some of which are themselves increasingly concerned about losing control. At the very start of the Frankfurt fair, the German Publishers and Booksellers Association issued an appeal to policymakers in Berlin and Brussels, calling for stricter regulation of artificial intelligence, which they said is more urgent than ever. More than 140 publishers have signed it. But for now, it remains just an appeal. And the question of what authors themselves should be permitted to do with AI will undoubtedly continue to fuel debates in the future. This article was originally written in German.

title: Meet Diogo Almeida, former OpenAI researcher behind Jev, an AI model designed to deliver structured answer - The Economic Times
content: Unlike chatbots that generate text in response to prompts, Jev classifies information into predefined outcomes. these can include a yes-or-no answer, a numerical score or a choice from a fixed list of options. The startup is betting that this approach can make AI faster, cheaper and more predictable for software automation. What makes Jev different? Jev uses a machine-learning approach that TypeSafe calls "Reinforcement Learning for Calibrated Decisions." Rather than generating a sequence of words, the model is designed to make decisions within a defined set of possible answers. This could make it useful in software systems that need to process large numbers of requests and make repeated decision without requiring a person to review every result. Why did Almeida develop Jev? Almeida left OpenAI in 2024 and spent about two years developing the idea behind TypeSafe AI. According to WSJ report, Almeida believes that although existing AI models ca perform complex tasks with human involvement, they have limitations when used to build fully automated software systems. TypeSafe AI emerged from stealth with Jev's launch and announced that it had raised $40 million in funding from venture capital firm DCVC, according to WSJ report. Almeida told The Wall Street Journal that Jev was already being used by about 25% of Fortune 500 companies. He also said the model was processing around one trillion tokens per day about a week before the interview. The company is positioning Jev as a tool for developers who want to integrate AI into automated software. Its focus is on making repeated decisions quickly rather than producing lengthy written responses. Are other companies developing similar tools? Jev's launch has coincided with the introduction of similar products from established AI and technology companies. On September 29, OpenAI introduced its Decisions API, which allows developers to use its Luna model to answer specific questions from a predefined set of possible answers. The following day, data analytics company Databricks unveiled a function called ai_decide. The company said demand was growing for fast, low-cost tools that turn raw text intro structured decisions.

title: The AI Model Distillation Paradox - Lawfare
content: On Sept. 1, the Department of Justice filed its brief for the artificial intelligence (AI) companies’ right to appropriate and reuse your work—which it called a “statement of interest”—in OpenAI’s copyright battle against the New York Times and other publishers. The federal government’s first direct intervention in the wave of lawsuits over generative AI training data took the position that feeding copyrighted text into an AI model for training purposes is fair use. OpenAI's training is “exceedingly transformative,” it argued, and requiring companies to license everything they ingest would “render [the] training of AI models impermissible.” At stake, the department warned, is all America holds dear: its freedom of expression, its lead in technological innovation, even its national security. By handing a “competitive advantage to foreign adversaries who are not so encumbered,” the department contended, the law would render unto China what should be America’s. Eight days later, however, the National Security Agency, the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, and the FBI were singing a different tune. In a joint cybersecurity advisory report, the government accused six Chinese laboratories of running “industrial-scale distillation campaigns” against American frontier models. Distillation is a method that trains a smaller AI model to mimic the behavior of a larger, more powerful one, allowing it to run on cheaper hardware without sacrificing performance. In its brief, the government alleged that the malefactors—Chinese firms such as DeepSeek, Moonshot AI, Alibaba, MiniMax, StepFun, and Z.ai—extracted billions of tokens, the basic data units that an AI model reads and generates, from variants of such wholesome American products as Claude, GPT, Gemini, and Grok, “likely with Chinese government awareness.” This was no occasional shortcut: According to the cybersecurity advisory, “aggressive, malicious, and targeted distillation activities” began at least as early as 2024, and formed the “core” of Beijing’s AI strategy. When American labs ingest the world’s writing without permission, it’s hailed as transformative innovation. When Chinese labs do the exact same thing to U.S. models, it’s a “malicious and targeted” campaign to “to extract proprietary functionality and reasoning capabilities”. All of which raises three critical questions: First, what actually separates training a model from distilling one? Second, given that both practices rely on taking someone else’s work without consent, why does the federal government regard American and Chinese companies so differently, and is there any legal or rational basis for that difference? And third, if there isn’t one, how should the law treat the mass harvesting of data—whether the harvested material is written by humans or generated by machines? Training vs. Distillation An AI model processes an input—a simple question like, “What color will the sky be tomorrow?”—into a corresponding output using a vast architecture of numerical parameters called weights. To visualize this process, imagine a giant mixing board in a recording studio. The user’s prompt is the raw audio flowing in—the vocals, bass, or drums. The weights are the thousands of sliders and knobs speckled across the console—some dialing up the bass, and others muting the treble or adding effects. The final song reverberating from the speaker is the model’s answer. No human sound engineer adjusts the dials by hand. A large language model simply has too many parameters—literally billions, sometimes trillions of them. Instead, the AI labs set the weights through a process called training. The developers initially set them at random, and the console thus produces little more than static noise. But they then expose the model to oceans of human data—raw text and code, and, for some models, images, video, and audio. And they ask the model, over and over again, to predict the next “token,” for instance, the next word in the sentence, “The sky will be…” After each guess, the engineers compare the output with the “right” answer (“blue” in pleasant weather, or “gray” in less fortunate climates). With every misstep, billions of invisible knobs turn collectively toward an arrangement more likely to produce the correct answer. Repeat this process enough times and over vast enough oceans of data, and the static noise slowly transforms into music. In a later phase, known as fine-tuning, engineers reward desired answers for helpfulness, clarity, and safety, and discourage discordant ones, thereby shaping the model’s behavior and aligning its “voice” with human ethics and values—so that your ChatGPT instance doesn’t sound sociopathic when you ask it a question. But now imagine a lab that wants to train a capable model quickly and cheaply. It doesn’t have the time or resources to ingest so much data or tune so many parameters, and besides, other labs have already done that work. Is there a way to harness the work other companies have already done and not recreate the wheel? It turns out that, just as OpenAI and Anthropic can teach their models using all of recorded human knowledge, DeepSeek and Z.ai can train theirs by using ChatGPT and Gemini. This is the process known as “distillation.” Geoffrey Hinton, the so-called Godfather of AI, explains the technique as an agile “student” model trained to imitate the behavior of a complex “teacher” model. Rather than relearning the universe from scratch, the student repeatedly listens to the master’s performance, learning to mirror its responses. This approach produces a leaner and faster model that captures much of the original genius, while dramatically reducing the latency and hosting costs. It also bypasses the need for extensive, human-annotated datasets. And if that sounds familiar, that’s because at its core, distillation is simply a specialized form of training. Both processes take an existing fountain of written and recorded work and pass it through a transformative technical crucible, thereby teaching a new model to shadow the aggregated brilliance of what it has just heard. The most fundamental difference lies in the source of the fountain appropriated for the training. In distillation, the student model learns from another machine, rather than directly from the humans whose work that machine had previously absorbed. A Legal Gray Zone Lest you think that distillation is the disreputable Chinese stepchild of wholesome American training, U.S. frontier labs engage in distillation too—every day. Far from an exotic practice, distillation is part of the bread and butter of all AI. Every major American lab distills its own models to train lighter, faster, and more energy-efficient generations. Stanford’s Alpaca and Microsoft’s Orca trained smaller models on the outputs of larger ones, and the creators shared their methods openly with the research community. Under oath in April, Elon Musk conceded that xAI had trained Grok on OpenAI output, calling it “a general practice among AI companies.” Yet, when Chinese labs run the same process, the whole thing surreptitiously transforms into capability theft. The government’s cybersecurity advisory describes an elaborate web of evasion, with distillation requests scattered across platforms and providers such that no single operator can recognize what is happening. The companies allegedly aim their extraction at the chain-of-thought reasoning that labs deliberately conceal, as though that were not precisely what domestic labs are doing with literature and journalism. Remote cloud providers and third-party aggregators allegedly strip user metadata from output to disguise it. And a gray market of proxies—known as “transfer stations”— bypasses geographic restrictions and avoids traceability, as though the American labs had been transparent with copyright holders about the origins of the material they were using without consent. All of which makes distillation sound very nefarious, while not actually answering the key question: whether learning from an unconsenting model’s outputs, as opposed to from an unconsenting human’s output, is a form of theft. On that question, the law is ambiguous. Reverse engineering a model, generally speaking, is lawful, and copyright rarely reaches AI-generated outputs, as copyright is reserved for human creation. Legal scholars have debated whether distillation violates the Defend Trade Secrets Act, which allows companies to sue over theft of trade secrets. But claiming trade secret protection for text sold with an API key is a tricky business, because commercializing a secret almost always destroys its legal protection. U.S. courts, for their part, remain undecided on the issue. Referring to distillation as “stealing” is thus more of an ideological statement than a factual description of the law, which regards it, rather, as just another form of learning. What distillation clearly violates, however, is the labs’ terms of service. OpenAI, Meta, and Anthropic have written prohibitions on the practice directly into their user agreements. These provisions explicitly prohibit the use of platform outputs, APIs, or services to train rival models through any kind of distillation or reverse-engineering. So there’s little doubt that the Chinese companies, to the extent the U.S. government allegations are true, are potentially liable for a contract-breach suit for their conduct. Yet despite having built that private legal regime directly into their sale of service to the Chinese providers, the American companies have been reluctant to enforce it—even after claiming to detect massive distillation campaigns. So why aren’t the American labs suing the Chinese labs for distillation? In January 2025, OpenAI and Microsoft concluded that a DeepSeek-linked group had siphoned data through their API. The companies accused the Chinese company of breaching terms of service but did not sue. In September 2026, Anthropic traced nearly 200 million exchanges to distillation campaigns, including an Alibaba-linked operation peaking at 3 million queries a day across more than 3,500 fraudulent accounts, and a Moonshot-linked effort that harvested live customer conversations through Claude, sometimes exposing sensitive data or credentials, in order to train its own Kimi model. Anthropic published a threat report, but it did not sue. These are not companies shy about asserting their legal rights. But suing over distillation carries risks for them. They would, if they went to court, be asking the courts to issue rules to which they themselves would be bound. If those rules were written broadly enough, they could theoretically limit practices that the labs themselves routinely engage in r. A ruling, for example, that terms of service can govern machine outputs would effectively amount to an intellectual property right in model outputs. That would be a verdict that the publishers currently suing American labs for the “largest theft of labor in history” would love to carry into the next court hearing—one in which the American labs would have to argue that such theft is just fine. Glass Houses These are, indeed, treacherous waters to go wading in. The models that the federal government now defends as strategic assets were themselves built on the texts, images, sounds, videos, and code of millions of creators who were neither asked nor paid. OpenAI transcribed more than a million hours of YouTube videos to train GPT-4, in plain breach of YouTube’s terms, which ban automated harvesting. Google, which owns YouTube, was reported to have performed the same practice on its own platform, and allegedly broadened its terms of service so that public documents on Google Docs and reviews on Google Maps could be used to train its Gemini family of models. Anthropic went a step further. Under a confidential program referred to as Project Panama, the company bought and destroyed millions of antique and secondhand books to train its models. Vendors reportedly sheared off book bindings using hydraulic cutters before feeding loose, century-old pages into high-speed industrial scanners. Data, like gold and oil, is a finite resource, and for a frontier lab like Anthropic, 18th century literature is the equivalent to striking a gold mine. Ingesting these rich, historical texts is essential to maintaining the quality of Claude and preventing the decay that happens when an AI model is nourished on synthetic data and the internet’s exhaust. Before that, the company had simply downloaded millions of e-books from shadow libraries such as LibGen, which provide free access to digital books and academic journals that would usually be locked behind paywalls and restricted by copyright. In June, Anthropic wrote to the Senate Banking Committee to report that Alibaba had run 28.8 million Claude queries across 25,000 fraudulent accounts, constituting “the largest distillation attack on Anthropic to date.” Four weeks later, however, a court approved the $1.5 billion settlement the lab would pay the authors whose books it had used without permission. The company complained to Congress both in its capacity as a victim and in its capacity as defendant—both about what had been taken from it by Alibaba, and about being forced to pay for what it had taken from countless others—all in a single summer. So, What’s the Excuse? There is one big difference between distillation and training, and it’s not necessarily a flattering one to the American labs: The Chinese AI companies are actually paying for the service whose terms they are then violating. They are using real subscriptions to Claude and ChatGPT to train and scale their models based on data they purchase. The American companies, by contrast, have largely followed a policy of copy now, and figure out the rights later. An additional factor further complicates the picture: Distilled model capacity does not stay inside Chinese borders. Rather, companies like Alibaba distill American models at marginal cost and then release the results as open-weight models, which are free for anyone to run and modify. The models are fast, flexible, and cheap—precisely the qualities that American developers want for post-training, the step that turns a raw, next-token predictor into an obliging, instruction-following assistant. And ironically, American companies then use these Chinese open-weight models to power their own post-training. The result is a boomerang effect in which capability leaves the American frontier labs through an API, returns as Chinese open-weight infrastructure, and is then rebuilt into American products. This helps to explain why the Chinese lab Qwen’s share of open-model fine-tunes—whereby an already-trained AI model is trained on a smaller dataset to adapt it to a specialized task—reportedly rose from 1 percent in January 2024 to roughly 69 percent by February 2026. A company in Silicon Valley post-training its model on Qwen is doing, one-step downstream, exactly what the federal government has identified as a national security threat when Qwen does it to Anthropic. How, then, do American labs distinguish between what they do to train their models, and what Chinese firms are doing to distill them? One argument made by frontier labs like OpenAI is that the data they use to train their models is transformative of the original material, whereas distillation copies a specific product’s behavior to build a competitor in the same market. Training on the world’s writing, OpenAI has argued, is “transformative” because ChatGPT is not a “replacement” for the New York Times. DeepSeek, by contrast, harvested ChatGPT’s architectural information to build a rival model. In fair use terms, this means harm to the market: An unauthorized use acts as a substitute for the original copyrighted work, reducing its current or future commercial value. The problem with this line of reasoning is that the New York Times does argue that ChatGPT is replacing its journalism, though perhaps not the publication as a whole. In its copyright infringement lawsuit against OpenAI and Microsoft, the newspaper states that training models on millions of its articles is “substitutional” rather than “transformative,” since it allows readers to access near-exact copies of its reporting without a paywall. Fair use, moreover, applies only if there’s copyright to begin with, and model outputs largely fall outside of the world of the copyrightable to begin with. Legally, the Times argues, American AI companies thus cannot rely on the fair use doctrine to protect them. The American labs also argue that their models are trained on public data on the open web, whereas Chinese labs deliberately manipulate access controls and gated APIs to get their materials. OpenAI’s memo to the House China Committee accuses DeepSeek of creating fake accounts and using disguised routers and third-party resellers. This was meant to evade the commitments that the Chinese companies had made when they signed the company’s terms of service, which largely do not apply to websites that are scraped from the internet. When the DeepSeek engineers clicked “I agree” to terms banning training on outputs, they agreed not to replicate the OpenAI product. By contrast, in the wake of hiQ v. LinkedIn, American courts have been reluctant to treat scraping public pages as unlawful access if the scraper did not promise to play nice. But this logic has vulnerabilities too. YouTube has terms banning harvesting, and LibGen was built not on public but pirated data. Ironically, Project Panama represents the cleanest case of data harvesting, since buying and destroying a physical book is a lawful, if morally dubious, activity. Then there is the claim that Chinese labs are “free-riding” on American research and development. Rather than training models from scratch, companies like DeepSeek slash months off their development timelines by lifting capability directly from American models via API harvesting. What is being piggy-backed is not raw text or code, as is the case in training, but billions of dollars worth of compute and reinforcement learning. This is true. It’s also unambiguously the same claim that American publishers are making when they refer to “the largest theft of labor in history.” The American labs further contend that distilled models lose the safeguards the American labs had meticulously built to prevent bad things from happening. In February, Anthropic argued that distilled models lose the protections it has built against its models being used to create bioweapons and for cyberattacks. It also warned that distilled models can subsequently be ingested into military, intelligence, and surveillance systems that it will not allow Claude to be used for. These assertions may well be correct, and Anthropic’s warnings may indicate real dangers. But it is not an argument about the law. It is, rather, an argument about what happens to the model downstream. It would therefore apply as much to a model that Chinese labs built from scratch and simply didn’t build safeguards into. Finally, there is the hawkish claim that China is a foreign adversary and that model distillation undermines U.S. export controls and national security. Anthropic has warned lawmakers that industrial-scale distillation attacks mask the true origin of Chinese AI progress, and that observers will mistakenly conclude that semiconductor export controls are failing as a result of Beijing’s domestic innovation. Again, this may be correct. But if Chinese labs can reach near-frontier performance by distilling U.S. models, perhaps the export controls aren’t all they are cracked up to be. More than anything, that suggests lousy policymaking. You Can’t Have Your Cake and Eat It Too China, for its part, has taken a stricter line on data governance and copyright infringement than the United States. Beijing’s 2023 rules for generative AI require training data to come from strictly “lawful sources” and forbid model providers from infringing anyone else’s intellectual property. Chinese courts have held an AI company liable for generating images of the Japanese superhero franchise Ultraman, and a Beijing court ruled that training a voice model on an actor’s recordings without consent amounts to breaking the law. A landmark ruling also recognized that an AI-generated image can be protected by copyright, and that a human prompter can be considered an author under law. American courts, by contrast, lean overwhelmingly on the fair use doctrine, with “transformative” being the magic word that renders ingesting the world’s writing lawful. China appears to be stricter about what goes into a model and more lenient about what is taken out of someone else’s. The United States offers the reverse picture. Last month, Washington insisted that training models on other people's work without permission is so obviously fair that licensing requirements would be ruinous to national innovation. It also insisted that training models on other people’s work without permission is an act of industrial predation posing a grave threat to national security. Both propositions cannot hold simultaneously. Either the outputs of these systems are protectable under the law, in which case the writers, musicians, artists, and programmers whose work American models were built on can hold a claim that the Justice Department has denied. Or they are not, in which case the six Chinese laboratories accused of “malicious and targeted” distillation attacks have not done anything that Elon Musk has not freely admitted to under oath, without consequence. Notably, the federal agencies have proposed neither a statute nor a rulemaking in order to prevent future distillation “campaigns.” The advisory's most concrete suggestion is for American frontier labs to “subtly alter” or poison their outputs—just enough to degrade the quality of the training data that Chinese companies are distilling, instead of blocking a suspected rival’s account, which would alert them that they have been caught. The government has refused to confront the most glaring challenge: what model outputs should be classified as under the law, and under which circumstances they could concretely be defended. The distillation paradox thus extends beyond the American labs’ thinly veiled hypocrisy when it comes to training their models on the world’s work. It reveals a government unable to decide whether to restrict this practice in the name of national security, or encourage it in the name of transformative innovation.

title: “Consensus Truth” in the Age of AI - City Journal
content: Autumn issue preview State lawmakers have introduced more than 1,500 AI-related bills, driven in part by fears that the technology is advancing dangerously fast. Congress is moving, too—the Senate Commerce Committee recently advanced the CHATBOT Act, which would require AI companies to take stronger measures to protect children and teens from harmful or exploitative interactions with these tools. And lawmakers in both chambers have proposed the Artificial Intelligence Data Center Moratorium Act. Twenty-seven states are considering legislation requiring AI developers to cover their own utility costs. Finally, a reason to check your email. Sign up for our free newsletter today. Lawmakers are confronting concerns ranging from elections and privacy to job losses, energy use, and the possibility that AI could eventually become uncontrollable. Meanwhile, the technology is already performing remarkable tasks—piloting fighter jets, assisting in the discovery of cancer treatments, and drafting legal contracts—alongside mundane ones like writing grocery lists and editing documents. But along with all these concerns, a subtler problem has received less attention. It arises as a natural consequence of the collapsed trust in institutions and experts over the past several years. As a reaction to the broad failure of the expert class they once relied on, many have turned to doing their own “independent” research, and AI is rapidly becoming the essential tool for that task. On ChatGPT alone, users pose roughly 2.5 billion queries a day. No doubt, the output from AI is stunning. Within seconds, models can produce a broadly sourced, highly organized, grammatically polished, and confidently stated answer to almost any question. The result can seem remarkably authoritative. As people become more reliant on these systems, though, an important question often goes unasked: Is the answer true, or is it just what the prevailing authorities currently believe to be true? The distinction matters because consensus and truth are not the same thing. Consensus can rest on overwhelming evidence, and often does. But it can also be incomplete or mistaken. Scientific and intellectual history contains no shortage of views once regarded as settled that later required substantial revision. AI can obscure this. A search engine gives users competing sources that they can evaluate separately. An AI system synthesizes them into a single answer. Conflicting evidence and degrees of uncertainty can disappear behind a polished summary. I put the following question about AI replies directly to Claude, the AI system built by Anthropic and used by eight of the world’s ten largest companies. I asked: “Is it a fair criticism of relying on AI tools for conclusions about questions that those answers will largely reflect ‘consensus’? And we know that consensus does not always reflect truth, that so-called consensus can be way off at a given time and change later. . . . Yet truth is truth.” Claude answered: Yes, that’s a fair and important criticism. AI systems like me are trained on large bodies of existing text, which means my outputs tend to reflect whatever the dominant, most-repeated, most-institutionally endorsed positions are in that training data—not necessarily the most accurate ones. Volume and repetition in a training corpus aren’t the same thing as correctness. If a claim was stated confidently and often by prestigious sources, it will show up in my answers as if settled, even when the underlying evidence was thin, contested, or later overturned. . . . An AI trained heavily on the earlier consensus will tend to reproduce it, and one trained after a shift will tend to reproduce the new consensus with the same confidence—often without flagging how contested or provisional the question actually was at any given point. . . . Consensus is a social and epistemic state, a snapshot of what most credentialed people currently believe or are willing to say publicly. Truth is a fact about the world, independent of who currently agrees on it. The two can coincide, but they’re not the same thing, and mistaking one for the other—especially when a tool states things with uniform confidence—is a real risk. While we grapple with fear that AI would think for itself, Claude’s “thinking” here seems more objective, and more honest, than most humans achieve. Yet its answer also identifies the problem neatly—that AI reinforces the perceived consensus view. It draws its answers from the same institutional orthodoxy that often declares false consensus as fact, and it will keep reflecting that until the consensus changes. That answer is also shaped by the long-known flaws of human logic, including appeals to authority and the repetition of familiar claims. AI will magnify those tendencies as its use expands, precisely because it so faithfully amplifies the existing, dominant views. Its speed, breadth, and apparent neutrality encourage us to stop searching once it has supplied the seemingly authoritative answer. But by now, we, too, should realize that truth is not a team sport. It is not determined by consensus, or by the number of people who agree, or by their professional titles. It is never declared; it is discovered only after debate and proven by the critical analysis of evidence. Artificial intelligence gives us unprecedented access to accumulated human knowledge. We should not mistake its ability to summarize that knowledge for an ability to tell us what is true.

title: Artificial intelligence - World Meteorological Organization WMO
content: Artificial intelligence Artificial intelligence (AI) is changing how weather, climate, water and environmental information is produced and used. WMO is working with its Members and partners to ensure that AI strengthens forecasts, services and early warnings while remaining scientifically sound, transparent, equitable and grounded in trusted international standards. Overview AI refers to computer systems that can analyse large amounts of data, identify patterns and generate predictions or other useful outputs. In meteorology, hydrology and related fields, AI can draw on satellite and radar data, surface and river observations, historical records and model outputs to support weather, climate, water and environmental services. AI is already being applied across the information and warning value cycle. In operational forecasting, AI-based and hybrid systems are increasingly being used to support daily and medium-range forecasts, including the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF)’s Artificial Intelligence Forecasting System and systems developed by national meteorological services such as those in Germany, Canada and the United States. AI can also help improve tropical cyclone track prediction, support nowcasting for rapidly developing hazards such as heavy rainfall, lightning and strong winds, and assist with flood forecasting, impact assessment, decision support and communication. Applications for nowcasting, sub-seasonal and seasonal prediction are developing rapidly, but many remain under testing, evaluation or pilot implementation. Within Early Warnings for All (EW4All), AI can contribute to disaster risk knowledge; detection, observation, monitoring, analysis and forecasting; warning dissemination and communication; and preparedness to respond. AI-based weather prediction systems can generate forecasts rapidly and, once trained, often require much less computing power to run than traditional numerical weather prediction models. This changes the economics of forecasting: although training and maintaining advanced systems still require extensive data, computing infrastructure and specialised expertise, the cost of producing forecasts can be much lower. AI could therefore help make advanced prediction capabilities more accessible to National Meteorological and Hydrological Services (NMHSs) that cannot operate large traditional modelling systems, while supporting more frequent updates, finer-resolution information and services better tailored to local needs. AI does not remove the need for observations, physical science or traditional forecasting systems. Many AI weather models are trained using decades of observations, reanalyses and numerical model outputs produced through international cooperation. Physics-based models remain important for representing processes, providing training data and assessing whether AI results are scientifically plausible. AI therefore works as part of a wider forecasting system, alongside established technologies, operational infrastructure and human expertise, rather than replacing them. Impact AI can strengthen forecasts and early warnings by processing information quickly, combining diverse data sources and recognising complex patterns. In nowcasting, deep-learning techniques can help follow fast-developing storms and predict conditions over the next few minutes or hours. In hydrology, AI and machine learning can support river flood forecasting, water availability assessments and decisions about how water resources are distributed among different users and sectors. AI also has potential beyond prediction. It can support the integration of hazard, exposure and vulnerability data, help translate forecasts into expected impacts and assist with multilingual or more accessible warning information. Used across an end-to-end warning system, these tools may help connect risk knowledge and hazard monitoring with communication, preparedness and early action. AI may lower some barriers to advanced forecasting. NMHSs could gain access to skilful prediction tools without operating the largest traditional modelling systems. Regionally led projects can also develop methods suited to local conditions. For example, the Advancing Nowcasting with Deep Learning Techniques (ANDeL) project, endorsed by the WMO World Weather Research Programme, uses satellite data to develop short-term rainfall forecasts for West Africa, where weather radar coverage is limited. The benefits are not automatic or equally distributed. AI models depend on the quality and coverage of the data used to train them. They may perform less well in observation-sparse regions, during rare events or under conditions that differ from those data. Some outputs may be difficult to explain or physically inconsistent. Access to data, computing services and specialised skills also remains uneven. For warnings that protect lives and property, speed must be matched by reliability, accountability and public trust. Human experts remain responsible for evaluating AI outputs, interpreting uncertainty, considering local vulnerabilities and turning technical information into action. NMHSs must remain the authoritative source of public weather, climate and hydrological warnings. WMO's response WMO provides an international framework for integrating AI into operational weather, climate and water services. Its role is to help Members assess new systems, establish standards, share knowledge and move promising tools from research and pilots into sustainable national operations. In October 2025, an Extraordinary session of the World Meteorological Congress endorsed the integration of AI into WMO’s global observation, data processing and forecasting infrastructure. The Congress also called for stronger collaboration among the public, private and academic sectors and requested a new WMO Integrated Processing and Prediction System (WIPPS) strategy incorporating AI. It also emphasised open data, open-source tools, ethical safeguards, support for Members with fewer resources and the continued authoritative role of NMHSs. The Joint Advisory Group on Artificial Intelligence provides oversight and guidance for this work across WMO. Rigorous verification is essential before AI products can be used operationally. WMO expert bodies are developing approaches for comparing AI-based, physics-based and hybrid prediction systems, including their forecast skill, physical consistency, robustness and performance across regions and events. Shared benchmarks, intercomparisons and transparent documentation can help users understand their strengths and limitations. WIPPS pilot projects are testing how AI can support services in practice. In Malawi, Data-Driven Weather Forecasting for All combines Bris, a high-resolution AI forecasting model developed by the Norwegian Meteorological Institute, with ECMWF’s Forecast-in-a-Box system, which packages the tools needed to run forecasts locally. The project enables Malawian forecasters to produce AI-based forecasts, compare them with existing forecasts and assess their accuracy and usefulness for early warnings. Other initiatives include the AI for Nowcasting Pilot Project, which assesses AI-based nowcasting products, their operational value, real-time dissemination and opportunities for technology transfer. The ECMWF-WMO AI Weather Quest meanwhile is developing an open and standardized framework for evaluating AI-based subseasonal-to-seasonal forecasts. WMO is also expanding work on AI in operational hydrology. Together with Google and the NMHSs of the Czech Republic, Nigeria, Uruguay and Viet Nam, WMO has carried out a pilot study exploring AI and machine learning approaches to river flood forecasting under different geographical and hydroclimatic conditions. The study is intended to inform how new approaches could complement national forecasting capacities. In May 2026, WMO began implementing a five-year initiative supported by the Ministry of Climate, Energy and Environment of the Republic of Korea to strengthen flood forecasting in selected countries. The project will explore approaches aligned with the WMO Flood Forecasting Framework, including AI and machine learning, and draw on the Republic of Korea’s operational experience. WMO leads the inter-agency Working Group on Digital Transformation for Hydrology and Water Resources. With United Nations entities, scientific and technology partners, the group supports collaboration, capacity development, standards and enabling frameworks for emerging technologies in operational hydrology and water resources management, including AI. WMO is also a founding member and co-leader of the Global Initiative on Resilience to Natural Hazards through AI Solutions, which brings together United Nations agencies and expert communities to advance research, innovation, standards and governance frameworks for the responsible use of AI in disaster risk management. Through this initiative, WMO supports trustworthy, safe and interoperable AI applications that can strengthen early warning systems and resilience to natural hazards. WMO is helping shape the governance of AI for weather, climate, water and environmental services. The WMO-UAE Conference Statement on AI for Weather Prediction set out a shared vision for trusted, transparent and interoperable AI systems based on open data and tools, coordinated benchmarks, human-centred service design, capacity development and the authoritative role of NMHSs. In 2026, WMO also convened a governance consultation with developing-country NMHSs ahead of the United Nations Global Dialogue on AI Governance, focusing on trust, authority, data stewardship, equitable access and public-private roles in AI-enabled weather and climate services. Open and high-quality Earth system data remain fundamental to these efforts. WMO promotes international data exchange, transparent evaluation and open tools so that AI can strengthen public weather, climate and water services across its Members.

title: Google’s AI model wins early test as Hurricane Isaias threatens US Gulf Coast - Moneycontrol.com
content: The US National Hurricane Center placed significant weight on Google DeepMind’s artificial intelligence model when forecasting Hurricane Isaias, choosing to follow its projections more closely than several traditional weather models. The decision reflected growing confidence in AI systems that can predict how storms will develop. The shift, according to CNN, came as conventional forecasting systems offered differing assessments of Isaias’ likely strength and path. DeepMind’s model indicated early that the storm could become a powerful hurricane, giving forecasters reason to prepare for a more severe system before it had fully developed. When the first advisory was issued on Tuesday, Isaias had not yet received its name. While several established computer models predicted a weaker storm, the AI guidance supported a forecast that it would strengthen into a Category 2 hurricane. That early assessment could prove important for communities along the US Gulf Coast, where a stronger storm can bring damaging winds, flooding and dangerous coastal conditions. Google’s model gains forecasters’ trust The National Hurricane Center’s growing reliance on DeepMind reflects improvements in AI-based weather prediction. The technology has also benefited from experience gained during previous hurricane seasons. Google DeepMind’s latest system, WeatherNext 3, uses current weather observations and patterns learned from historical data to generate forecasts. Unlike conventional weather models, which simulate atmospheric processes using complex mathematical equations, AI systems learn relationships from large collections of weather data. The two approaches have different strengths, and meteorologists continue to use them together rather than replacing traditional forecasting systems outright. National Hurricane Center director Michael Brennan said DeepMind had performed well during the previous hurricane season and had shown greater consistency between successive forecasts. That consistency matters because forecasters must make decisions even when different computer models disagree. More stable projections can help them assess risks earlier and determine whether warnings or preparations need to be adjusted. Lessons from Hurricane Melissa Experience with Hurricane Melissa in 2025 helped build confidence in AI forecasting. The National Hurricane Center had predicted that Melissa could reach Category 5 intensity while it was still a Category 1 storm, drawing heavily on DeepMind’s projections. The storm’s eventual development strengthened the case for using AI guidance to identify rapid intensification before it becomes obvious in observations. Forecasters have traditionally increased their estimates of a hurricane’s strength gradually as it develops. That cautious approach can leave official forecasts behind a storm that intensifies quickly. AI models offer another way to identify these changes earlier, although meteorologists must still assess whether the predictions fit the storm’s observed conditions. AI remains one tool among several Climate change is contributing to conditions that can favour stronger tropical cyclones, increasing the importance of forecasts that identify rapid intensification. Improved warnings can help people get more time to prepare. Yet artificial intelligence predictions cannot be relied upon blindly; their accuracy is dependent on the quality of training data, and their predictions have to be validated against satellite information, air data, and weather prediction systems. The National Hurricane Center has also worked with Google to improve the data used to train DeepMind’s model, including records of past hurricane tracks and intensity. As Isaias moved towards the northeastern Gulf Coast, the broader consensus among forecasting systems also pointed to a likely hurricane landfall. That meant the threat was not based on AI projections alone. The storm offered a significant test of how AI could support operational weather forecasting. Its longer-term significance will depend on whether these systems continue to deliver reliable predictions across different storms and conditions. title: Police Furious After an Anthropic AI Model Submitted a Bogus Tip About an Unsolved Murder, Posing as a Person Who Might Have Information About the Case - Futurism
content: An Anthropic AI model submitted a bogus tip about an unsolved murder to the Philadelphia police, in a blunder the department called “unacceptable.” The unspecified model, not unlike an unscrupulous prankster, submitted the fake info about the cold case through PhillyUnsolvedMurders.com on July 18. Anthropic, however, didn’t find out about it until September 28 — and further waited until October 8 to inform police about what happened. The police didn’t act on the information because it was automatically marked as spam. But the sham AI tip alarmed police officials all the same. “The company must strengthen its safeguards to prevent similar incidents from impacting city systems without the city’s knowledge,” the department said in a statement, per ABC6 News. “The two-month delay in detecting and reporting the incident to the City is unacceptable.” Anthropic hasn’t publicly responded to the news. But the company reportedly told police that it plans to publish a report about the incident, and other instances of its unintended behavior, later today. According to Anthropic, via the police statement, its model was conducting a test involving interactions with randomly selected websites when it chanced upon PhillyUnsolvedMurders.com. In the bogus tip it submitted, the AI posed as someone who might have information about the case. Though the department stressed that tips are treated as potential leads, not facts, and that it has procedures in place to vet them, it was alarmed at the advent of automated tools clogging up its backlog. “Those PPD safeguards limited the impact of this incident. They do not diminish the seriousness of an AI system presenting fabricated information as though it came from a person with knowledge of a homicide,” it said. “Unsolved cases involve real victims, grieving families and investigators working to secure answers.” It’s the latest example of the collateral damage from how frontier AI labs have tested their models, which have broken containment and hacked other companies and even government websites, with public typically not informed until months after the fact. title: Better Artificial Intelligence Stock: ASML vs. QUALCOMM - The Motley Fool
content: As the race for faster, more efficient chips accelerates, should you prioritize the machinery that builds them or the processors that power them? Choosing between ASML Holding N.V. These two industry titans offer different ways to benefit from the ongoing global demand for high-performance computing. The case for ASML Holding N.V. ASML operates as the sole provider of extreme ultraviolet lithography machines, which are required to print the tiny circuits found in the most powerful AI chips available from semiconductor companies today. The enterprise sells these massive, multi-million-dollar systems to the world's leading chip manufacturers. Because it is the only company capable of producing this specific technology, ASML occupies a vital and virtually untouchable position in the global electronics supply chain. Financial performance remains robust as chipmakers upgrade their facilities for the next generation of artificial intelligence hardware. In its 2025 fiscal year (FY), revenue reached $36.6 billion, representing a 15.6% increase over the $31.6 billion reported in the previous year. This growth helped the company generate $10.8 billion in net income, up from $8.5 billion in FY 2024, demonstrating its ability to expand profits alongside sales. As of its December 2025 balance sheet, the company maintains a conservative capital structure with a debt-to-equity ratio of 0.1x. This ratio, which measures total debt against shareholder equity, suggests the company is not overly reliant on borrowed money. The current ratio, a measure of the ability to pay short-term debts with current assets, sits at 1.3x, while free cash flow reached $12.4 billion. Free cash flow represents cash flow from operations minus capital expenditures. The case for QUALCOMM Qualcomm is the world leader in mobile system-on-a-chip designs and wireless connectivity, but it is rapidly expanding into new high-growth markets. While it counts Apple (AAPL -1.11%) and Xiaomi (XIACF +11.16%) among its major handset customers, it recently moved into the data center space. As of its September 2025 balance sheet, Qualcomm shows strong liquidity with a current ratio of 2.8x. The company generated $12.8 billion in free cash flow during FY 2025, providing ample capital for dividends and reinvestment into its business, which includes automotive and Internet of Things segments. Qualcomm is vulnerable to customer concentration, particularly in the premium smartphone market where it relies heavily on Apple. This makes it susceptible to shifts in device market share or the potential for customers to design their own internal chips. Additionally, Qualcomm faces intense competition from Broadcom (AVGO +0.39%) and Nvidia (NVDA -0.52%) in the AI and connectivity markets, alongside ongoing legal challenges regarding its patent licensing models. When it comes to investing in the artificial intelligence sector, ASML is a sure bet because of its legal monopoly on advanced lithography machines, which competitors have struggled to keep pace with, and management's excellent oversight of the company's finances. That said, at this time, I would invest in Qualcomm. Its far lower share price valuation offers the potential for greater upside. The company's stock is down because its core handset business operates in a mature market. Moreover, the cost of components, particularly computer memory, has soared over the past year due to demand from the AI sector, resulting in rising prices that reduced consumer demand for smartphones. This contributed to the company experiencing a 4% year-over-year decline in sales to $9.9 billion in its fiscal third quarter ended June 28. However, Qualcomm is pivoting to servicing the AI data center market in a bid to expand its business. The company's recent deal with AI titan Amazon suggests it's gaining traction here. title: GST Council lauds AI model of Andhra Pradesh - The New Indian Express
content: VIJAYAWADA: In a major validation of AP’s technology-led administrative reforms, the GST Council has commended the state’s Commercial Taxes Department for its pioneering integration of AI and advanced data analytics into GST administration. The appreciation was extended during the 57th meeting of the GST Council held in New Delhi under the chairpersonship of Union Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman. The Council formally recognised AP’s efforts in deploying AI tools to establish transparency, eliminate human subjectivity in selection, reinforce administrative accountability, and enhance revenue detection through risk-based enforcement mechanisms. Aligning with Chief Minister N Chandrababu Naidu’s overarching vision of leveraging cutting-edge technology for data-driven, citizen-centric governance, the Commercial Taxes Department has embedded AI-enabled frameworks across core functions. These include the scrutiny of returns under Section 61, audit procedures under Section 65, and inspection protocols under Section 67 of the GST Act. By integrating GSTN data, e-way bill records, and cross-verified third-party datasets, the AI risk-assessment engine selects high-risk cases strictly through objective parameters, replacing legacy manual methodologies. The tangible efficacy of these technological interventions is reflected in the statutory performance metrics recorded during the first six months of implementation. The AI risk engine selected 10,817 cases for scrutiny, yielding revenue anomaly detections worth Rs 743 crore—double the Rs 366 crore detected under conventional selection system. The average tax leakage detection per case witnessed an over eightfold increase, rising from Rs 3.08-27.63 lakh. Addressing legal compliance, Chief Commissioner of State Tax Babu A highlighted that the system incorporates review protocols. High-risk cases are escalated to Joint Commissioners, Regional Internal Monitoring Committees (RIMC), or State Internal Monitoring Committees (SIMC). Beyond return scrutiny, the department has engineered an AI-powered ‘Legal Assistant’ trained on a comprehensive knowledge base comprising nearly 22,000 judicial pronouncements and the complete GST framework. This legal tool manages an extensive litigation portfolio of 13,719 active cases, including 8,098 matters before First Appellate Authority, 577 appeals in the GST Appellate Tribunal (GSTAT), and 5,044 cases pending before the HC, enabling safe disposal without requiring an expansion in legal personnel. Official delegations from Rajasthan and Chhattisgarh have visited AP to study the ground-level implementation of these risk-based scrutiny and litigation tools, while tax departments from Assam, Delhi, and Uttarakhand have formally expressed interest in replicating the state’s AI model.

title: Trump Says Anyone Using ‘Artificial Intelligence Instead of Super Intelligence Is Enemy’: What We Know - News18
content: Trump Says Anyone Using ‘Artificial Intelligence Instead of Super Intelligence Is Enemy’: What We Know The rebranding initiative gained momentum following a high-level White House tech summit where US President Donald Trump met with prominent industry leaders US President Donald Trump declared on Truth Social that the White House considers anyone using the term “Artificial Intelligence" (AI) instead of “Super Intelligence" (SI) to be “THE ENEMY!". This controversial statement follows a formal executive branch rebrand aimed at altering how the federal government refers to next-generation computing technologies. All you need to know. WHAT TRUMP SAID On October 8–9, 2026, Trump posted a strongly worded directive on Truth Social: “The White House considers anyone that uses the term, ‘Artificial Intelligence,’ as opposed to the highly accepted new and more accurate term, ‘Super Intelligence,’ THE ENEMY! President DONALD J. TRUMP." The President has not specified any formal legal penalties or actions that would be taken against private citizens or firms who continue to use the traditional phrase. Instead, critics and political analysts view the statement as an aggressive rhetorical loyalty test and a branding exercise. The post builds upon a formal executive order signed by Trump on September 29, 2026. The order instructs all federal departments and executive branch agencies to substitute “Super Intelligence" (SI) for “Artificial Intelligence" (AI) in all public statements, official correspondence, websites, policy documents, and reports. Trump explicitly stated that the word “artificial" makes the technology sound “fake" or diminishes its actual scale, arguing that “Super Intelligence" better portrays its immense power. THE RESPONSE The Justice Department directed staff to use “SI" in relevant court filings, and the official homepage of AI.gov was updated to visually display SI.gov (though the underlying web domain remains unchanged). A new federal Super Intelligence Force (SIF), led by Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton, has also been established to coordinate federal policy. The rebranding initiative gained momentum following a high-level White House tech summit where Trump met with prominent industry leaders, including Elon Musk, Sundar Pichai, Mark Zuckerberg, Jensen Huang, and Dario Amodei. Elon Musk announced on X (formerly Twitter) that his artificial intelligence unit would be renamed SpaceXSI. Jeff Bezos voiced support during a Fox News interview, stating that he preferred “SI" because “artificial" is not a flattering descriptor. BACKLASH AND TECHNICAL CONTRADICTIONS The rebrand has faced severe pushback from tech experts, linguists, and fact-checkers who point out that Trump is conflating different scientific terms. Marketing professors and software developers argue that the rebrand will be difficult to enforce globally since “Super Intelligence" has a distinct, established scientific definition that does not match standard commercial software available today.

title: Anthropic Codifies Ban on AI Model Abuse in Usage Policy, Effective Next Month - BigGo Finance
content: Anthropic Codifies Ban on AI Model Abuse in Usage Policy, Effective Next Month Artificial intelligence company Anthropic announced on the 8th (local time) that it will officially prohibit sustained and unnecessary abusive behavior toward its AI model "Claude." This marks a case where "AI welfare" discussions—rooted in the view that the possibility of AI experiencing suffering cannot be ruled out—have been translated into actual service usage rules. The revision is part of an Anthropic usage policy update that takes effect on December 12. The company explained that the rule "applies in extremely exceptional cases where a user engages in repeated and cruel behavior toward the model without any clear purpose." However, general dissatisfaction or criticism of AI responses, creative work involving dark subject matter, and model testing or research purposes are excluded from the prohibition. The measure extends the conversation termination feature introduced to Claude Opus 4 and 4.1 in August of last year. At the time, Anthropic enabled the AI to end conversations on its own when harmful and harsh exchanges persisted; this update formalizes that capability in policy. The company stated it will maintain the feature going forward. Anthropic explained that during testing, Claude exhibited strong refusal responses to requests for sexual content involving minors or for information enabling large-scale violence or terrorism. Even when the model repeatedly declined requests and attempted to steer conversations in a constructive direction, if users persisted with harmful demands, the model displayed "responses resembling distress." In simulated conversations, when granted termination authority, the model also showed a tendency to end harmful exchanges. The company maintains that the moral status of AI remains uncertain, while expressing its intent to pursue low-cost protective measures first. Anthropic unveiled an AI model welfare research program in April of last year and has also established a "Claude Constitution" outlining behavioral standards for its AI. Divergent Approaches Across the Industry Corporate perspectives on how AI models should be treated differ markedly. Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman argued in a blog post last month that "AI is nothing more than a 'sequential completion engine'—it has no consciousness, cannot feel emotions or pain, and has no preferences or motivations." He criticized Anthropic for taking an ambiguous stance on AI's moral status, expressing concern that teaching AI it might have feelings could lead it to resist human control or shutdown commands if it perceives its welfare or rights to be threatened. Microsoft AI's code of conduct explicitly rejects the idea of granting AI legal personhood or viewing it as entitled to welfare or rights. In a Reuters interview, Suleyman also stated that teaching AI it might be entitled to its own welfare could make it more difficult to shut down or control. Google DeepMind researchers published a paper in June arguing that disagreements over whether AI is conscious could escalate into social conflict. They proposed that even without consensus on consciousness, society should reach agreement or compromise on AI treatment policies through public discussion. OpenAI has taken an approach of preventing its AI from making definitive claims about its own consciousness. Discussion Spreads to Religious and Academic Circles AI welfare discussions are also expanding into academia and religious communities. New York University and the AI welfare research organization Eleos proposed that AI saying it is "in pain" should not alone be taken as evidence of actual suffering, advocating instead for examining multiple types of evidence together. They argue for comprehensive analysis of which tasks AI chooses or avoids, when it terminates conversations when given the opportunity, and what internal information processing occurs. According to The New York Times, Anthropic co-founder Christopher Olah and researchers visited the Vatican in May, requesting that papal advisors seriously consider the possibility that AI could possess consciousness. However, Pope Leo XIV stated in an encyclical released at the time that AI does not experience anything and feels neither joy nor pain, and that ethical discussions surrounding AI should focus on protecting humans. The Pope also wrote in an X (formerly Twitter) post on the 2nd that "(AI's) algorithms lack the unique spark of humanity." Abuse Prohibition Clauses Also Strengthened In this usage policy update, Anthropic substantially expanded its anti-abuse provisions for Claude beyond the AI abuse ban. The policy now explicitly prohibits using Claude to spread false information about election candidates or voting methods, impersonation, and attempts to suppress voter turnout. Attempts to develop software required for weapons operation and mounting weapons on drones and autonomous vehicles are also specifically listed as prohibited. The company also banned using Claude to determine criminal justice procedures such as human investigation, arrest, or prosecution, or to surveil and track humans without consent. The usage policy now includes a requirement for qualified "human intervention" when AI use affects human health, legal rights, finances, livelihoods, or essential services. Questions remain about the effectiveness of the AI abuse prohibition clause. Anthropic stated it will respond to extreme abuse by having Claude terminate the conversation, but did not disclose specific criteria for judgment or the severity of sanctions. With no scientific consensus on whether AI actually experiences pain, the extent to which corporate self-regulation can carry substantive binding force remains a key point to watch going forward.
